title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: On my return, I found the following letter from my father:
"My dear Victor,

"You've probably been waiting impatiently for a letter setting the date of your return. I was tempted at first to write just a few lines mentioning when to expect you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I can't do it. What would your surprise be, my son, if instead of a happy welcome you found tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you about our tragedy? Absence can't have made you indifferent to our joys and sorrows. How shall I deliver such pain to my long-absent son? I want to prepare you for the terrible news, but I know it's impossible. Even now your eye is racing across the page, searching for the words that will tell you the horrible truth.
"William is dead! That sweet child whose smiles warmed and delighted my heart, who was so gentle yet so full of life! Victor, he was murdered!
"I won't try to console you. I'll simply describe what happened.

"Last Thursday, May 7th, I went walking in Plainpalais with my niece and your two brothers. The evening was warm and pleasant, and we stayed out longer than usual. It was already getting dark before we thought about heading home. That's when we realized William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be found. We sat down to wait for them. Soon Ernest came back and asked if we'd seen his brother. He said they'd been playing together, that William had run off to hide, and that he'd searched for him in vain and waited a long time, but William never came back.

"This alarmed us. We kept searching until nightfall, when Elizabeth guessed he might have gone home. He hadn't. We went out again with torches. I couldn't rest knowing my sweet boy might be lost, exposed to the damp and cold of night. Elizabeth suffered extreme anguish too. Around five in the morning, I found my lovely boy — whom I'd seen just the night before, so full of life and health — lying on the grass, pale and motionless. The murderer's fingermarks were on his neck.

"He was carried home. The anguish on my face gave away the secret to Elizabeth. She desperately wanted to see the body. I tried to stop her at first, but she insisted. Entering the room where he lay, she quickly examined the victim's neck. Clasping her hands, she cried, 'Oh God! I've murdered my darling child!'

"She fainted and was revived only with the greatest difficulty. When she came to, she could only weep. She told me that the same evening, William had begged her to let him wear a very valuable miniature portrait she had of your mother. The picture is gone. It was undoubtedly what lured the murderer to the deed. We have no trace of him yet, though we're searching tirelessly. But nothing will bring back my beloved William!

"Come, dearest Victor. You alone can console Elizabeth. She weeps constantly and blames herself, unjustly, as the cause of his death. Her words pierce my heart. We're all miserable. But won't that be one more reason for you, my son, to come home and comfort us? Your dear mother! Alas, Victor! I find myself saying, thank God she didn't live to see the cruel, miserable death of her youngest child!

"Come, Victor — not with thoughts of vengeance against the murderer, but with feelings of peace and gentleness that will heal, rather than worsen, our wounds. Enter this house of mourning, my friend, with kindness and love for those who care about you, not with hatred for your enemies.
"Your affectionate and afflicted father,
"Alphonse Frankenstein.
"Geneva, May 12th, 17—."

Clerval had been watching my face as I read. He was startled to see the despair that replaced the joy I'd first shown at receiving news from my friends. I threw the letter on the table and covered my face with my hands.
"My dear Frankenstein," cried Henry, seeing my bitter tears, "must you always be unhappy? My dear friend, what's happened?"
I motioned him to read the letter while I paced the room in extreme agitation. Tears streamed from Clerval's eyes too as he read the account of my tragedy.
"I can offer you no comfort, my friend," he said. "Your loss is beyond repair. What do you plan to do?"
"Go to Geneva immediately. Come with me, Henry, to arrange the horses."

As we walked, Clerval tried to say a few consoling words. He could only express his deepest sympathy. "Poor William!" he said. "Dear, lovely child. He sleeps now with his angel mother! Who that saw him — so bright and joyful in his young beauty — could help but weep at his untimely loss! To die so horribly, to feel the murderer's grip! How much worse that someone could destroy such innocent radiance! Poor little fellow! We have one consolation: his friends mourn and weep, but he is at rest. The agony is over. His suffering has ended forever. He's covered by earth now and knows no pain. We can no longer pity him. We must save that for his miserable survivors."

Clerval said this as we hurried through the streets. His words impressed themselves on my mind, and I remembered them later in solitude. But for now, as soon as the horses arrived, I jumped into a carriage and said goodbye to my friend.

My journey was deeply sad. At first I wanted to hurry, longing to console my loved ones. But as I approached my hometown, I slowed down. I could barely endure the flood of feelings crowding into my mind. I passed through scenes familiar from my youth, scenes I hadn't seen in nearly six years. How much might have changed in that time! One sudden, devastating event had struck. But a thousand small circumstances might have worked other changes — quieter ones, but no less significant. Fear overcame me. I didn't dare go forward, dreading a thousand nameless horrors I couldn't define.

I stayed two days at Lausanne in this painful state of mind. I gazed at the lake. The water was calm. Everything around was peaceful, and the snowy mountains — "the palaces of nature" — were unchanged. Gradually the calm, heavenly scene restored me, and I continued toward Geneva.

The road ran alongside the lake, which grew narrower as I approached home. I could see the dark slopes of the Jura more clearly, and the bright summit of Mont Blanc. I wept like a child. "Dear mountains! My own beautiful lake! How do you welcome your wanderer? Your peaks are clear, the sky and lake are blue and still. Is this a promise of peace, or are you mocking my unhappiness?"

I'm afraid, my friend, that I'll bore you by dwelling on these details. But they were days of relative happiness, and I think of them with pleasure. My country, my beloved country! Only a native can know the delight I took in seeing your streams, mountains, and above all, your lovely lake!

Yet as I drew closer to home, grief and fear overwhelmed me again. Night was falling. When I could barely see the dark mountains, I felt even gloomier. The landscape seemed like a vast, dim scene of evil. I sensed that I was destined to become the most wretched of human beings. Alas! I prophesied truly, and failed only in one thing: in all the misery I imagined and dreaded, I didn't conceive a hundredth part of the anguish I was destined to endure.

It was completely dark when I reached the outskirts of Geneva. The city gates were already shut, so I had to spend the night at Secheron, a village about a mile and a half away. The sky was clear. Unable to rest, I decided to visit the spot where poor William had been murdered. Since I couldn't pass through town, I crossed the lake by boat to reach Plainpalais. During the short crossing, I saw lightning playing on Mont Blanc's summit in the most beautiful patterns. The storm seemed to be approaching quickly. When I landed, I climbed a low hill to watch its progress. It advanced. The sky clouded over. I soon felt large drops of rain, and its violence quickly increased.

I left my seat and walked on, though the darkness and storm grew worse by the minute. Thunder crashed directly over my head with terrific force. Echoes bounced from Mont Salêve, the Juras, and the Alps of Savoy. Vivid lightning flashes blinded me, illuminating the lake like a vast sheet of fire, then plunging everything into pitch darkness until my eyes could recover. The storm appeared in several parts of the sky at once, as often happens in Switzerland. The most violent part hung exactly north of the town, over the part of the lake between the headland of Belrive and the village of Copêt. Another lit up the Jura with faint flashes. A third alternately revealed and hid the Môle, a peaked mountain east of the lake.

While I watched the tempest — so beautiful yet so terrifying — I walked on quickly. This noble war in the sky lifted my spirits. I clasped my hands and cried aloud, "William, dear angel! This is your funeral. This is your requiem!" As I said these words, I spotted a figure stealing from behind a clump of trees near me. I stopped and stared. I couldn't be mistaken. A flash of lightning illuminated it clearly: its gigantic height and the deformity of its appearance, more hideous than any human face. I knew instantly that it was the wretch, the filthy demon to whom I had given life. What was he doing there? Could he be — I shuddered at the thought — the murderer of my brother? No sooner did that idea cross my mind than I was certain of it. My teeth chattered. I had to lean against a tree for support. The figure passed quickly and vanished into the darkness. Nothing in human form could have destroyed that innocent child. _He_ was the murderer! I was sure of it. The mere thought carried irresistible proof. I considered chasing the devil, but it would have been hopeless. Another flash revealed him clinging to the rocks of the nearly vertical face of Mont Salêve, a hill that borders Plainpalais to the south. He quickly reached the summit and disappeared.

I stood motionless. The thunder stopped, but the rain continued. The scene was wrapped in impenetrable darkness. I turned over in my mind the events I had tried to forget: the entire course of my journey toward the creation, the appearance of my handiwork at my bedside, its departure. Nearly two years had passed since the night he first received life. Was this his first crime? Alas! I had turned loose upon the world a depraved wretch whose joy was in slaughter and misery. Had he not murdered my brother?

No one can imagine the anguish I suffered through the rest of that night, spent cold and wet in the open air. But I didn't feel the weather. My imagination was consumed with scenes of evil and despair. I thought about the being I had cast among humanity, endowed with the will and power to carry out horrors like the deed he had just committed. I saw it almost as my own vampire, my own spirit let loose from the grave, forced to destroy everything dear to me.

Day broke, and I headed toward town. The gates were open. I hurried to my father's house. My first instinct was to reveal what I knew about the murderer and have him pursued immediately. But I hesitated when I considered the story I'd have to tell. A being I myself had created and given life had met me at midnight among the cliffs of an inaccessible mountain. I also remembered the nervous fever that had seized me just after the creation — a detail that would make an already impossible story sound like pure madness. I knew that if anyone else had told me such a tale, I'd have dismissed it as insane. Besides, the strange nature of the animal would let it escape any pursuit, even if my family believed me enough to begin one. And what would be the point? Who could arrest a creature capable of climbing the overhanging sides of Mont Salêve? These thoughts made up my mind, and I resolved to stay silent.
It was about five in the morning when I entered my father's house. I told the servants not to wake the family and went to the library to wait for the usual hour of rising.

Six years had passed — lived as a dream except for one indelible mark — and I stood in the same spot where I'd last embraced my father before leaving for Ingolstadt. Beloved and revered parent! He still remained to me. I gazed at the portrait of my mother that hung above the mantelpiece. It was a historical painting, commissioned by my father, showing Caroline Beaufort in an agony of despair, kneeling by her dead father's coffin. Her clothes were simple, her cheek pale, but there was an air of dignity and beauty that barely permitted pity. Below this painting was a miniature of William. Tears flowed when I looked at it. While I stood there, Ernest entered. He'd heard me arrive and rushed to welcome me. "Welcome, my dearest Victor," he said. "Ah! I wish you'd come three months ago. You would have found us all joyful and happy. You come now to share a misery nothing can ease. But your presence will, I hope, revive our father, who seems to be sinking under his grief. And maybe you can persuade poor Elizabeth to stop her endless, tormenting self-blame. Poor William! He was our darling and our pride!"

Uncontrolled tears fell from my brother's eyes. A sense of mortal agony crept over me. Before, I'd only imagined the wretchedness of our destroyed home. Now reality hit me as a new, equally terrible disaster. I tried to calm Ernest and asked about my father and then about my cousin.
"She needs consolation most of all," said Ernest. "She's accused herself of causing my brother's death, and that's made her terribly unhappy. But since the murderer has been discovered—"

"The murderer discovered! Good God! How? Who could possibly pursue him? It's impossible — like trying to outrun the wind or stop a mountain stream with a straw. I saw him too. He was free last night!"

"I don't know what you mean," replied my brother in confusion. "But for us, this discovery has completed our misery. No one wanted to believe it at first. Even now Elizabeth won't be convinced, despite all the evidence. Who would have thought that Justine Moritz — so kind and devoted to the whole family — could suddenly commit such a horrible, appalling crime?"
"Justine Moritz! Poor, poor girl — she's the accused? But it's wrong! Everyone must know that. Surely no one believes it, Ernest?"

"No one did at first. But several things came to light that have almost forced us to believe it. And her own confused behavior has added weight to the evidence. I'm afraid it leaves no room for doubt. But she'll be tried today, and then you'll hear everything."

He then told me that on the morning William's murder was discovered, Justine had fallen ill and been confined to bed for several days. During this time, a servant examining the clothes she'd worn that night found the portrait of my mother in her pocket — the miniature that was thought to be the murderer's motive. The servant immediately showed it to another, who went straight to a magistrate without telling the family. Based on their statements, Justine was arrested. When confronted with the evidence, the poor girl's extreme confusion only deepened the suspicion.
This was a strange story, but it didn't shake my belief. I replied firmly, "You're all wrong. I know who the murderer is. Justine, poor, good Justine, is innocent."

At that moment my father entered. I saw deep unhappiness on his face, but he tried to welcome me cheerfully. After we'd exchanged our sad greetings, he would have changed the subject, but Ernest exclaimed, "Good God, Papa! Victor says he knows who murdered poor William."
"Unfortunately, we do too," replied my father, "for I would rather have remained ignorant forever than discover such depravity and ingratitude in someone I valued so highly."
"My dear father, you're mistaken. Justine is innocent."
"If she is, God forbid she should suffer as guilty. She's to be tried today, and I sincerely hope she'll be acquitted."

This calmed me. I was firmly convinced that Justine — and indeed every human being — was guiltless of this murder. I had no fear that any circumstantial evidence could be strong enough to convict her. My own tale was impossible to tell publicly. Its astounding horror would be dismissed as madness by ordinary people. Apart from me, its creator, did anyone exist who would believe — unless they saw it with their own eyes — in the living monument to arrogance and reckless ignorance that I had let loose on the world?

We were soon joined by Elizabeth. Time had changed her since I'd last seen her. She was more beautiful than in her girlhood. She had the same sincerity, the same liveliness, but paired with an expression of deeper intelligence and feeling. She welcomed me with the greatest warmth. "Your arrival, dear cousin," she said, "fills me with hope. Perhaps you'll find some way to prove my poor Justine innocent. Alas! Who is safe if she's convicted? I believe in her innocence as firmly as I believe in my own. Our misfortune is doubly hard. We've not only lost our lovely darling boy, but this poor girl — whom I sincerely love — faces an even worse fate. If she's condemned, I'll never know joy again. But she won't be. I'm sure she won't. And then I'll be happy again, even after the sad death of my little William."
"She is innocent, my Elizabeth," I said, "and that will be proved. Don't be afraid. Take heart from the certainty of her acquittal."
"How kind and generous you are! Everyone else believes she's guilty, and that made me hopeless — because I knew it was impossible. Seeing everyone else convinced of it left me in despair." She wept.
"Dearest niece," said my father, "dry your tears. If she is, as you believe, innocent, trust in the justice of our laws and in my determination to prevent the slightest hint of unfairness."
